title: A Range You Can Index, Count and Loop Over
oneLiner: Write StepRange, a lazy range of numbers from start to stop by step, that supports a count, indexing, membership tests in O(1) and looping, without ever storing its numbers.
keyTakeaway: A collection doesn't have to store its items: compute them. Count, indexing and membership are arithmetic, so they're O(1) even for a billion numbers. In C# that means a Count property, an indexer and an IEnumerable<int> iterator; in Python, __len__, __getitem__, __contains__ and __iter__. Without your own Contains or __contains__, the language falls back to looping through every item.
explanation:
Write a class StepRange(start, stop, step) for the numbers start, start + step, start + 2 * step, ... up to and including stop if it's reached. StepRange(1, 10, 3) is 1, 4, 7, 10 and StepRange(1, 9, 3) is 1, 4, 7. step is always 1 or more, and if stop is less than start the range is empty. It must support: the number of items (Count in C#, len() in Python); indexing, range[i] for 0 <= i < count, which must throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException (C#) or IndexError (Python) for any other i; a membership test (Contains(x) in C#, x in range in Python); and looping with foreach / for.

Don't store the numbers: one test uses StepRange(0, 2000000000, 2), which has a billion items. The count is (stop - start) / step + 1 when stop >= start (use long arithmetic in C# to be safe, as the difference can exceed int.MaxValue), item i is start + i * step, and x is in the range when start <= x <= stop and (x - start) is divisible by step. Each test reports [count, the items as a list (only when there are 20 or fewer), the membership results for the probe values, range[0] or "error", and range[count] or "error"].

In C#, implement IEnumerable<int> with a yield-based GetEnumerator plus the non-generic one, a Count property, an indexer public int this[int i] and a Contains method. Without your own Contains, range.Contains(x) quietly uses LINQ's version, which loops over all billion numbers. In Python, write __len__, __getitem__, __contains__ and __iter__; without __contains__, in falls back to iterating.

testCases.expectedJson: [1000000001, "too many to list", [true, false, true, false], 0, "error"]

visualizationSteps.message: Nothing is stored: these four numbers are computed when asked for. Count = (10 - 1) / 3 + 1 = 4.
Indexing is arithmetic: item 2 is 1 + 2 * 3 = 7. Index 4 would be past the end, so it throws.
Membership is arithmetic too: 5 is between 1 and 10, but (5 - 1) % 3 isn't 0, so it's not in the range. O(1), no loop.
Looping yields start, start + step, ... one at a time, so even a billion-item range costs no memory.

complexity.note: Count, indexing and membership are arithmetic on start, stop and step, so they're O(1) however long the range is, and nothing is stored. Looping over all n items is O(n) time, still O(1) space.
